O. Henry. Born William Sydney Porter, an American short-story writer celebrated for witty, sentimental tales of working-class and bohemian life in New York City.

Writing under a pseudonym—allegedly after a pharmacist friend—O. Henry became a master of the plot twist and the sting in the tail. Stories that reverse expectations in the final lines and reward close reading. His warmth toward his characters' foibles, his ear for vernacular speech, and his prolific output made him one of the most widely read American writers of his era.

His signature stories have become American classics. "The Gift of the Magi" shows a young married couple each selling their most prized possession to buy the other a Christmas gift, only to discover the gifts are now useless. "The Last Leaf" presents a sick woman who believes she will die when the last ivy leaf falls, and her neighbour paints a leaf on the wall to save her. "The Ransom of Red Chief" features would-be kidnappers tormented by their young captive and forced to pay the parents to take him back. And "A Municipal Report" begins as a dismissal of Nashville's dullness and becomes a story of quiet heroism and hidden nobility.

O. Henry perfected what became known as the O. Henry twist—a final revelation that inverts the story's apparent meaning without feeling contrived. He was a master of the working-class heroine. Manicurists, shop girls, stenographers treated with genuine dignity. He combined sentimental warmth with ironic distance. His sentimentality is never mawkish because it coexists with clear-eyed social observation. He wrote roughly two hundred fifty stories in his lifetime, often to meet magazine deadlines. This sheer productivity added to his popularity and accessibility.

O. Henry arrived in America's Gilded Age just as the short story was gaining cultural dominance over the serialised novel. His timing and sensibility made him a perfect fit. New York's immigrant working classes needed chroniclers, and O. Henry gave them stories where their lives mattered. His sentimentalism—the belief that kindness and dignity exist even in poverty—was radical in an era of naturalism's cold determinism. Though later critics would dismiss him as sentimental and facile, his best stories have proved durable because they balance cynicism and hope with genuine skill. In quiz bowl, O. Henry represents American populism, the magazine-story tradition, and the twist-ending as formal device.
